metadata.title: feat: add experimental Rust MCP runtime and session core
metadata.author: crivetimihai

description:
## 🔗 Related Issue
N/A

---

## 📝 Summary
This PR adds an experimental Rust MCP runtime and incrementally moves the MCP transport, high-volume JSON-RPC routing, and the first session/event-store slices into Rust while keeping the Python implementation available behind feature flags.

Key changes:
- add `tools_rust/mcp_runtime` and integrate it into `Containerfile.lite`, `docker-compose.yml`, and the managed entrypoint flow
- route public `/mcp` traffic through Rust with explicit runtime visibility in `/health`, `/ready`, startup logs, and MCP response headers
- narrow `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/*`, `prompts/*`, and several other MCP methods off the generic Python dispatcher
- wire the official `modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk` behind a feature flag for the upstream `tools/call` client path
- add feature-flagged Rust session metadata and Redis-backed event-store/session sharing, including dedicated session cleanup for server-scoped `DELETE`
- extend the load-test harness and document the runtime boundary, configuration, and migration status in `tools_rust/mcp_runtime/README.md` and `tools_rust/mcp_runtime/STATUS.md`

This remains intentionally reversible:
- full Python fallback: `EXPERIMENTAL_RUST_MCP_RUNTIME_ENABLED=false`
- Rust transport/runtime only: disable `EXPERIMENTAL_RUST_MCP_SESSION_CORE_ENABLED` and `EXPERIMENTAL_RUST_MCP_EVENT_STORE_ENABLED`

---

| Load benchmarks | Mixed MCP and tools-only Locust runs on the compose-built stack | ✅ |

Performance highlights on the compose-built Rust stack:
- mixed MCP workload: `1007.35 RPS` at `120` users, `1033.01 RPS` at `150` users, `0%` failures
- tools-only hot path: `1126.96 RPS` overall and `1068.5 RPS` on `MCP tools/call [rapid]` at `125` users, `0%` failures

## 📓 Notes
Current boundary:
- public MCP transport now flows through Rust
- Python still remains the control plane for auth/RBAC and some session/transport internals
- the runtime is intentionally feature-flagged so deployments can fall back to the Python path at any time

Follow-on work after this PR is the remaining transport/session ownership: replay/resume behavior, session existence/owner checks on the public path, and multi-worker session-affinity forwarding.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body:
this file should be broken up in a number of files, leaving only the entrypoint for the lib in `lib.rs` to improve human/agent redability

something like:
- src/main.rs: App entry & server initialization.
- src/routes/: Route definitions (merging sub-routers).
- src/handlers/: Request/response logic (HTTP layer).
- src/models/: Data structures & Serde structs.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: This session ownership check treats any` is_admin` token as globally authorized. Elsewhere in the codebase, admin bypass is only allowed when the token is unscoped (`teams == null`); team-scoped admins should still be restricted. The Rust runtime should mirror the same token-scope semantics here.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: This introduces a second DB access layer in Rust alongside the existing Python one. That means schema and auth/visibility semantics now have to stay aligned across both implementations. Can we converge on a single shared data layer instead of maintaining two?

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: This query duplicates Python-owned DB/business logic in Rust. I’m worried about long-term drift every time migrations or filtering rules change. It would be safer to either keep this behind the Python DB/service layer or move to one Rust DB layer that Python also reuses.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: The internal Python -> Rust proxy is configured with `follow_redirects=True`. Since this hop carries forwarded auth/context headers, transparently following redirects increases the chance of leaking trusted headers to an unintended target and hides misconfiguration. This internal sidecar hop should fail closed on redirects instead.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: The health path counts active sessions with Redis `KEYS`, which is a blocking full-keyspace scan. That makes `health` O(N) in the number of matching session keys and can become expensive under frequent probes or larger deployments. A maintained counter or a bounded `SCAN` style approach would avoid turning health checks into Redis hot spots.

comments.author: lucarlig
comments.body: Each resumed SSE connection runs its own poll loop against Redis, sleeping and replaying repeatedly until the session disappears. Functionally this works, but it creates steady per-connection Redis load for idle streams, so the cost scales linearly with open resumable connections. A push/notify-based wakeup would scale much better here.

comments.author: gandhipratik203
gandhipratik203
comments.body:
Since the Rust runtime is still marked **experimental**, should `httpx.HTTPError` fall back to `python_fallback_app` instead of returning a hard **502**?

Right now, if the sidecar is **down or restarting**, `/mcp` becomes fully unavailable even though a working Python path is already wired up and used on **lines 79 and 84** for other cases.

A graceful fallback on transport error would make **rollout and recovery safer** – operators could enable the Rust runtime without it becoming an **all-or-nothing risk**.

Example:

```python
except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
    logger.warning("Rust MCP runtime unavailable, falling back to Python: %s", exc)
    await self.python_fallback_app(scope, receive, send)
    return
```

If the hard **502** is intentional (to make sidecar failures visible rather than silently hiding them), ignore this comment 

OR

a configuration flag such as:

```
EXPERIMENTAL_RUST_MCP_RUNTIME_FALLBACK_ON_ERROR
```

could give operators the choice between **strict failure** and **graceful fallback**.

comments.author: gandhipratik203
comments.body:
The session read path currently performs a `GET` followed by a separate `EXPIRE` to refresh the TTL (lines **3322–3325**). This has two issues:

1. **Two round-trips on every session lookup** – one `await` for the read and another `await` for the refresh.
2. **Non-atomic behaviour** – if the key expires between the two calls, the session is returned to the caller but its TTL is never refreshed, silently leaving it closer to expiry than expected.

Since the project already uses `redis:latest` (Redis **7.x**), the `GETEX` command is available and combines both operations into a single atomic call:

```rust
let payload: Option<String> = redis::cmd("GETEX")
    .arg(&key)
    .arg("EX")
    .arg(state.session_ttl().as_secs())
    .query_async(&mut redis)
    .await
    .ok()
    .flatten();
```

This keeps the hot path to **one Redis round-trip** and removes the atomicity gap.

comments.author: gandhipratik203
comments.body:
`serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&message_json).unwrap_or(Value::Null)` silently converts a decode failure into a **null payload** that gets pushed into the replay response as a normal event. On a resume/replay path this feels risky – corrupted or partially written data becomes indistinguishable from an intentional `null` message and the stream continues without any signal that something went wrong.

There is also an inconsistency with **line 3851** – a missing key is already handled with `continue` (skip the event), but a corrupt payload takes the opposite path and emits it as `null`. In Rust, preserving the `Result` here usually gives safer semantics than recovering to a sentinel value.

At minimum, logging the decode error before skipping the event would make failures observable:

```rust id="qgqj3t"
match serde_json::from_str::<Value>(&message_json) {
    Ok(message) => events.push(EventStoreReplayEvent { event_id, message }),
    Err(err) => warn!("event store replay: skipping corrupt event {event_id}: {err}"),
}
```

comments.author: gandhipratik203
comments.body:
Since this is going in as an **experimental opt-in with improvements to follow**, just noting this here as a **possible direction for future performance improvements** if and when this path is optimised further.

The natural next step on the performance side could be **offloading async work** — session state sync, audit logging, metrics — onto **Redis Streams**, which the PR already uses for the event store. Keeping that pattern consistent would allow the synchronous **Rust → Python** path to remain lean without requiring any transport changes.

If payload size becomes a bottleneck later, **MessagePack** could be a relatively low-effort drop-in replacement for JSON, with mature support in both `rmp-serde` (Rust) and `msgpack` (Python).

If MessagePack is not sufficient and raw throughput needs to compete with other Rust-native MCP gateways, **Protobuf** (`prost` in Rust, `betterproto` in Python) could be considered as a further step, though it would require upfront schema definitions and code generation on both sides.

| Option                          | Effort | Gain   | Best for                                                                 |
|---------------------------------|--------|--------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Redis Streams for async offload | Medium | High   | Session sync, audit, metrics                                             |
| MessagePack over HTTP           | Low    | Medium | Reducing hot-path payload size                                           |
| Protobuf                        | High   | High   | Future use — if competing on raw throughput with other Rust-native MCP gateways justifies the investment |

I initially tried the permissive approach, but on second review that felt too risky because it can silently lose replayed events. So the final behavior in this PR is:

- corrupt replay payloads also no longer get silently skipped

comments.author: gcgoncalves
comments.body:
AI generated suggestion:

When a session is created without auth (unauthenticated request, `owner_email=None`) and `session_auth_reuse_enabled=false` (the default, which also clears `auth_binding_fingerprint`), both guards are inactive. Any caller that knows (or guesses) the `session_id` can access the session unchecked by Rust's layer. Subsequent callers could then re-initialize with their own auth and bind their credentials to the session, effectively stealing it.

comments.author: gcgoncalves
comments.body:
AI generated comment:

Clients can inject a `session_id` in the initialize payload, targeting an existing session. Combined with the ownerless bypass above, this enables a targeted session takeover when `session_core_enabled=true`. No length or format validation either (no UUID check, no max length bound), making this also a potential vector for oversized Redis keys.

What I verified:

- The broad "session stealing" claim does not reproduce on the normal auth-required stack.

    - so this is shared MCP/session compatibility behavior, not something newly introduced by the Rust path

What is still true:

- In permissive/public MCP mode, custom client-chosen initialize session ids plus ownerless-session semantics are worth reviewing more
  carefully.

I did not change that behavior in this PR because:

I tracked that narrower concern in tools_rust/mcp_runtime/FOLLOWUPS.md as a coordinated Python+Rust follow-up around client-supplied
initialize session ids / ownerless public-session semantics.

comments.author: crivetimihai
comments.body:
Thanks, I checked this one closely too.

A few important clarifications:

- This is not Rust-only behavior.
    - Python already accepts client-supplied initialize session ids as well.
    - So this is a shared compatibility choice, not something newly introduced by the Rust runtime.
- On the normal auth-required stack, I could not reproduce authenticated takeover.
    - first caller initializes with a chosen session id
    - second caller targeting the same id is denied with -32003 Access denied

So I did not remove this behavior in this PR.

What I do agree with:

- custom client-supplied initialize session ids are more security-sensitive than server-emitted opaque ids
- the current behavior has no explicit UUID/length validation on the Rust side
- in permissive/public MCP mode, this deserves a broader design review together with ownerless-session semantics

Because this is shared Python/Rust behavior and not a confirmed new Rust regression, I left it as follow-up rather than changing protocol behavior late in this PR. I tracked it in tools_rust/mcp_runtime/FOLLOWUPS.md as a coordinated Python+Rust cleanup around client-supplied initialize session ids, validation, and public-session semantics.

reviews.author: lucarlig
reviews.body:
Interesting PR, i love the general idea of rust components being fully independent. However I have been working on the `a2a_service` in https://github.com/IBM/mcp-context-forge/pull/3250, and one of the main challenges in fully replacing the Python service in this case is how the database layer is handled. The current Python implementation already contains assumptions around schema management, migrations, connection handling, and ORM/query behavior. Re-implementing or partially replacing that logic can easily introduce inconsistencies (e.g., differences in transaction handling, migration state, connection pooling, or query semantics), which makes the database layer particularly tricky to replicate safely.

Using a Python fallback may not provide the same feature set, safety guarantees, or performance characteristics. It could also behave differently under load, which makes this approach quite risky for production use.

if this PR were merged and then integrated with the changes introduced in https://github.com/IBM/mcp-context-forge/pull/3161, it would benefit from an existing and more robust CI setup. For that reason, I would recommend working toward merging https://github.com/IBM/mcp-context-forge/pull/3161 first and placing this implementation within the `crates` folder so it can leverage that infrastructure.

reviews.author: lucarlig
reviews.body:
I’m a bit concerned about the long-term architecture here. The Rust runtime is no longer just a transport edge; it now depends on an implicit contract with the Python backend across internal headers, internal endpoints, duplicated auth/session semantics, and direct DB knowledge. That works for a staged migration, but it also means changes to Python routing, token-scope behavior, or payload/header shapes can silently break Rust unless both sides evolve in lockstep.

The DB path has a similar issue. Right now migrations and schema ownership still live in the Python ORM/Alembic layer, while Rust is starting to read the same schema directly and reimplement some of the filtering/visibility logic itself. That creates two sources of truth for data access semantics. Every schema change or business-rule change now has to be maintained in both languages, which is going to get harder over time.

I think it would be healthier to converge on one shared boundary instead of growing both layers independently: either keep Python as the single DB/business-logic layer and expose a narrower internal API to Rust, or move the DB/data layer into Rust and have Python consume that same layer as well. The second option is more work, but it avoids permanent duplication and gives us a cleaner path to Rust-side performance gains.

reviews.author: araujof
reviews.body:
Nice work @crivetimihai ! This review focuses on any potential regressions or interactions with the Plugin Framework. 
 
### Summary

**No plugin framework regressions identified.** The Rust runtime integration is cleanly separated from plugin execution via the `has_hooks_for` guard. The only semantic change affecting plugins is the `prompt_id` UUID→name switch in post-hook payloads, which aligns with the pre-hook behavior and is unlikely to affect any plugin in practice.

### Test Results

| Suite | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Plugin framework unit tests | **All passed** |
| Service unit tests (tool/prompt/resource) | **All passed** |
| New sentinel plugin tests | **All passed** |
| Plugin performance profiling (31 plugins) | **All profiled, 0 errors** |

Performance numbers are consistent with baseline. No degradation detected.

### Findings

**1. Plugins bypass in Rust path**

`tool_service.py` — `prepare_rust_mcp_tool_execution` correctly falls back to Python when any tool plugin hooks are configured:

```python
if self._plugin_manager and (self._plugin_manager.has_hooks_for(ToolHookType.TOOL_PRE_INVOKE)
    or self._plugin_manager.has_hooks_for(ToolHookType.TOOL_POST_INVOKE)):
    return {"eligible": False, "fallbackReason": "plugin-hooks-configured"}
```

The Rust hot path is only taken when no tool hooks are registered.

**2. `prompt_id` UUID→name switch**

In `prompt_service.py`, `PromptPosthookPayload.prompt_id` changed from `prompt.id` (UUID) to `prompt.name` (string)

**Before:** `PromptPosthookPayload(prompt_id=str(prompt.id), result=result)`
**After:** `PromptPosthookPayload(prompt_id=prompt.name, result=result)`

All plugins use `prompt_id` for logging, passthrough in modified payloads, or as a Cedar/OPA policy resource identifier. No plugin parses it as a UUID. The pre-hook already uses the caller-supplied `prompt_id` (name or ID string), so this change actually **improves consistency** between pre-hook and post-hook — both now carry the human-readable prompt name.

**3. New internal MCP handlers correctly propagate plugin context**

The new `handle_internal_mcp_*` functions in `main.py` all extract `plugin_context_table` and `plugin_global_context` from `request.state` and pass them through to service methods. This matches the existing pattern in `handle_rpc`.

**4. `resource_service.py` server-scoping and `MultipleResultsFound` handling**

The resource service changes add server-scoped queries and handle `MultipleResultsFound` gracefully. These changes are upstream of plugin hooks (the plugin hooks fire after resource resolution). No interaction with plugin execution.

**5. `_load_invocable_tools` refactoring**

The extraction of tool lookup logic into `_load_invocable_tools` is purely structural. The existing `invoke_tool` now calls this helper, and the new `prepare_rust_mcp_tool_execution` also calls it. Plugin invocation in `invoke_tool` is untouched.
